newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metalworkers reach pay deal in Hesse.
newsitem.headline: German metalworkers reach pay deal in Hesse.

text.p: German metal and engineering trade union officials and employers said on Wednesday they had reached a pay deal for the some 400,000 workers in the regions of Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate and the Saar.

Following an agreement signed earlier for some 600,000 workers in the southern region of Nordwuerttemberg, the new accord means that wage deals have been signed for virtually all of the 3.2 million workers in Germany's metal and engineering sectors.

Moreover, all of the regional deals signed fail to implement a new law cutting sick pay from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent, an issue which has provoked mass protests in the industry and led to threats of all-out strikes next year.

Karl-Guenther Kronawitter, chief negotiator for the IG Metall trade union in Hesse, said the maintenance of full sick pay within the wage accord represented "the successful defence of an important social-political achievement".

Employer representatives, which had been hoping to achieve labour cost savings, were less enthusiastic about the deal, saying the terms had largely been set by agreements already reached in other areas of the country.
Earlier in Stuttgart, metal and engineering employers in Nordwuerttemberg said they had agreed a 1997 wage deal for the some 600,000 workers in the industry there.

Both of the new pacts mirror a break-through agreement reached in the northern state of Lower Saxony deal earlier this month in that workers will receive a 1.5 percent pay rise in 1997 and a further 2.5 percent increase the year after.
In return for allowing sick pay to be retained at 100 percent of salary, companies will be allowed to make small cuts in other areas, such as existing holiday or Christmas bonuses.

While such a package means that overall labour costs in the metal and engineering sectors will rise by less than one percent next year, it means that yet again employers will have failed to make the cost reductions they have been crying out for.
Meanwhile wage talks in the German construction industry also began in Frankfurt but were also not expected to reach agreement today.
The union IG Bauen-Agrar-Umwelt has said one of its key objectives is to battle seasonal unemployment which soared to 400,000 workers last winter.
"We will not even come close to nearing an agreement today," Klaus Wiesehuegel, head of the union said.
